messages:
Claire (AE): New RFP from Meridian Fin: they want a Private/VPC POC. Requirements: single /29 allowlist for egress, no route-table edits if possible, preserved client source IP for fraud scoring, and clear wording for their security questionnaire. Can we scope a solution?
Ethan (Solutions): Two viable patterns: (A) Customer-hosted connector in their VPC (preserves src IP, supports BYOIP egress), or (B) PrivateLink interface endpoint -> our connector. PrivateLink avoids route edits but control-plane egress still comes from Redwood EIPs unless connector runs in their account.
Mei (NetOps): If they insist on a single /29, we can provide an EIP block to allowlist. Note: centralizing egress via our EIP(s) will SNAT traffic and the customer will not see original client IPs. For zero route-table change, PrivateLink is the only way; app teams only need to update SGs.
Diego (Security): For the questionnaire, provide a short paragraph they can paste. Also flag TLS inspection: if their inline appliance removes SNI, our hostname routing may fail unless they allow passthrough or trust our cert.
Ethan (Solutions): Paste-able text for the questionnaire (short):

"Network Architecture (Private/VPC POC): Redwood supports two deployment patterns. Option 1 - Connector deployed in the customer's VPC: recommended when preservation of client source IP or BYOIP egress is required. The connector communicates outbound to Redwood control plane via TLS (TCP/443). Option 2 - AWS PrivateLink (Interface VPC Endpoint): minimal routing changes; interface ENIs are created in customer subnets and application traffic terminates on those ENIs. Required network changes: update security groups to allow app->endpoint TLS (443) and allow outbound TLS (443) from the connector to Redwood control-plane EIPs (we provide ranges during onboarding). If a customer requires fixed egress IPs, Redwood can provide a small set of EIPs for allowlisting; note that using shared Redwood-managed EIPs will SNAT connections and will not preserve the original client source IP unless the connector is customer-hosted."

Mei (NetOps): Quick SG examples to paste into runbook:
# allow app subnet to reach endpoint ENIs
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-app --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 10.11.12.0/24
# allow connector outbound to control-plane (example /29 allowed range)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-egress --group-id sg-conn --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 203.0.113.16/29

Ethan (Solutions): MTU note for their network team: if they have SD-WAN or IPsec tunnels lowering MTU, we can enable MSS clamping on the connector host:

iptables -t mangle -A POSTROUTING -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu

Diego (Security): Add to questionnaire: logging/forensics note: to ensure fraud systems see true client IPs, confirm whether traffic lands on an ALB/NLB (which may add X-Forwarded-For) or directly on backend instances. We'll need to validate during POC.
Claire (AE): Procurement Q: delta vs Dedicated + onboarding fees? Keep it high-level here.
Ethan (Solutions): High-level: POC with customer-hosted connector = one-time onboarding + platform license (connector infra paid by customer). Managed connector with reserved EIPs = onboarding + monthly connector charge; expect ~1.1-1.3x hosted costs for a small POC. I'll produce a short appendix for procurement.
provision-bot: POC workspace created: redwood-poc-meridian-2026 (id poc-mr-404). Link: https://internal.redwood/pocs/poc-mr-404
Mei (NetOps): I'll DM the exact EIP /29 we'll offer for the POC and recommended healthcheck TTLs (suggest 30-60s).
Claire (AE): Thanks all. I'll send the questionnaire snippet and SG examples to Meridian and ask for SD-WAN MTU + whether they terminate TLS at perimeter.
